I'm not sure if they stood guard in the proper sense of the word. We didn't have that sort of thing in Zelenike or in Kriz. There was no electricity, no public lighting. It wasn't safe to walk around the village at night. There was a risk of being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did people in the home guard wear uniforms, these elderly people?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, not those that guarded the village. There was a unit guarding Kracko Polje. They were wearing uniforms, but those were younger people aged between 40 and 50. Those who had not been sent to the front lines, were either sick or they were -- they weren't fit to carry firearms or maybe for some other reason they weren't allowed to go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did the people in the home guard carry weapons or partake and any military exercises?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I could just ask if those questions be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: First, did the members of the home guard, these elderly people, did they carry any weapons?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Those who were at Kracko Polje, this was not the front line, they were at the rear guarding the roads and the junction. They were carrying firearms, Marko Rajic, Glibo, Pavo Grubesas. Those elderly people, Ivan Ljubic, Kata's husband, they had rifles and uniforms, but I don't think Domin did and those other people over there who were killed. Domin's brother, Franjo, he had a uniform and a rifle, he was born in 1939 or possibly 1940. He was a member of the home guard. Ivan, Pavo, they stood guard in Kracko Polje, but they didn't go to Komin or to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was Domin ever sent to Kracko Polje?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, no. He wasn't fit for anything like that. He would get drunk on brandy and he would usually take a while to sober up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, did the elderly people in the home guard partake in any military exercises?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, no exercises. They were mostly peopled aged around 50 or 55, people who had previously worked in Croatia or in Split or in Sarajevo, and once the war began they were out of work. So they returned home. The command decided not to send these people to the front lines, so they said they could guard their own villages to see to it that no mines were laid along any of the roads; so that's what they ended up doing. There was a platoon of them, or a squad possibly. I'm not sure what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, may the witness be shown a video, V000-2719, which is 65 ter number 174? Since the E-court system doesn't show videos, we're going to show small clips. It's a two-hour-plus video -- no, no, we're not going to show two hours, Your Honour. I see that frown. It's a two-hour video. Only approximately 35 minutes, maybe 36 or 37, concern the killings in Uzdol. Of that we have about ten minutes in a group of small clips that we want to show the witness for identification of the bodies. And no interpretation, although there is a transcript which goes with it, no interpretation is necessary because we're only going to be identifying the bodies. In addition, for the Court's notice, I've told the witness we were not going to show the situation in his own home of his parents and his daughter. We are going to skip over that, and I've notified the Defence of that, too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 312.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: That was Domin's son, Ivo, and his wife Ivka. Four or five metres from them there was Zora Zelko's [phoen] body. It was all around Domin's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P312.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified earlier that you were the registrar of the village of Uzdol. What does the registrar do?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What do you do as registrar?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, you register the births of children, children who are born in my territory, my local commune, and the local commune of commune [as interpreted]. The local commune of Scipe also has a register so that we complemented each other. He would marry couples up there, and I would marry couples in Uzdol. He would register newly born children up there, but the old books up until the war were in Uzdol. If necessary, he would contact me if it was necessary to issue something or he would come to see me to obtain the relevant number. We would register children born, marriages, people who had died. We would issue death certificates in order to solve property issues, et cetera. There were lists of recruits of individuals who had to be vaccinated, lists of children who had to enroll in the first class in school, et cetera. Those are the sorts of duties that a registrar is involved in. For people in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland, we issue international certificates in 12 or 13 languages, and there are lists on family situation for people who are living abroad, et cetera. And there are similar international certificates of foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, do you maintain a book of the deaths that occurred or just deaths in general that have occurred in the village of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, we have original books. Each village has a new book now. We have eight books, eight original books. One is kept for Uzdol; there's another for Donja Vas; the third one is for Kranjcici; the fourth one is for Ljubunci; the fifth one is for Here, the sixth one is for Kute; the seventh one is for Scipe; and the eighth one is for Ivanci and Pajici. These are two villages, but they were small villages so there was just one book for these two villages. And there's a Donji and Gornji Kranjcici, but there was one book for Donji and Gornji Kranjcici. There were eight books, eight for births, eight for deaths, and one for marriages. When you use up one book, a new one is used. And the municipality certifies these books. These are original books. They are thick books, and the old ones are preserved. Our office has been in existence since 1956. We have some very old books, but new books have been introduced. But up until 1957 there was one book. After 1957, the villages -- there were books for eight various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, the persons who were killed on September 14th, were their names placed in any of these eight books?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: They were all born there. Serafina Stojanovic was born in Konjica, but she got married in Uzdol. She was married in Uzdol and she's registered in the book in Uzdol. But most of the others were -- all of them were born in Uzdol. My mother was born in Kranjcici, but she got married in Uzdol. That's where they were married. And my mother and the daughter were all registered there in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But were their deaths listed in the book of deaths in -- at the Uzdol registry?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Everyone from Uzdol lived in the territory of Uzdol, and they were all listed in the book of deaths for Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were death certificates ever issued for any of the individuals, any of these persons that were killed on --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. When they went to Split they wanted to know the exact information. They wanted to know when they were born. Then I didn't look into this. Then they were buried in the cemetery in Prozor. They remained there for eight or nine years, I suppose. There is a law according to which a body has to remain buried for a certain period of time. All the bodies were then put in Uzdol. Now there is an old cemetery from the old church in Uzdol and they were all buried there. They were all buried there two or three years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, has anyone ever requested death certificates for the 29 victims in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: They requested them when we entered a phone line. First they said that if there was civilian victims, we wouldn't have to pay for the telephone line, but we had to pay. But they said that it would be free. However, when it was introduced, everyone had to pay. Only the soldiers didn't have to pay that duty, as they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who requested the death certificates?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, the telephone exchange in Mostar requested them and then the municipality in Split requested it. An office also requested it. Certain civilian victims of the war were supposed to receive compensation, but this was delayed. Some civilian victims in Croatia retained some compensation, but in Bosnia only soldiers received such compensation. According to what I have heard via the Sarajevo news, it will only be next year that such compensation will be provided. And it will be necessary to provide a death certificate if request is being made for such compensation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, who in your village or who at your registry signs the death certificates?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The death certificates -- I sign the death certificates. When someone dies, I have to register this. Someone comes to inform me of the fact - his brother or father - and I issue the certificates and sign them because I'm the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at some death certificates. P -- it's a 65 ter number, 180. 0219-5695 to 0 --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, you have the number. Born on the 25th of May the 158, that's the municipality of Prozor; 553, that's the number that is issued by MUP, they issue that number. We then enter this into the book of marriages, births, and deaths. The registry number was only issued in the 1980s. Before, we didn't have these identification numbers. First you have the year, the month, and then the municipality, and then you have the MUP number below. You have the place of birth, place of death is Uzdol. Born in Kranjcici but married in Uzdol. Her father was Ljubic Toma [phoen]; mother Mazul Luca. Zelenika Jozo was the husband. He died before the war. She was buried at the time in Prozor. Now, if I was to issue a new death certificate, now they've been buried in Uzdol. Their bodies were transferred there after nine years. Now, Prozor would no longer be place of burial; it would be Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that your name and signature on the bottom right?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the registrar's signature. Then you have the number, Uzdol, and the date when it was issued. And you have the municipality's stamp. We don't have our stamp now, but up until the war we did. But Konjic, Prozor, Jablanica, they don't have these stamps anymore; I don't know why. They -- these certificates are certified elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like me to read off the 29 of them? There's a group of 41 here; we're just going to use the 29 that are listed in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you like and if there's no objections from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm just not sure about the 41, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What they did was they had 29 civilians and there were 12 HVO soldiers that were killed on that day in Uzdol. So they've listed all 41 -- they've included in that exhibit all 41 persons that been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in my submission it would be appropriate to put in all the 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I would like to offer that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit P313.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's be a good time for us to take a break. We'll have a 30-minute break and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey. Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Could I just indicate to the Court that having considered the matter since the break, I indicate that we will not be in a position to finish the cross-examination today. I suspect we will probably go -- we won't take up all of tomorrow by any means, but we will go into tomorrow. Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zelenika. Mr. Zelenika, at the time of these incidents, by which I mean in early of September of 1993, the village of Uzdol was effectively on the front line of combat operations between the HVO and the Bosnian army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what's the particular name of the part of Uzdol where the school is based?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Cer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that Uzdol is the general name for that area. Is there a particular part of that area which is also called Uzdol or is Uzdol just simply a general name?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There are several hamlets, Rajici, Medesi [phoen], Bobari, Pale, Kriz, Zelenike, Zelici, that's about it. There are two or three houses further down, the Maric's house, the Stojanovic's house, Budim, but it's all part of Uzdol, four or five hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. So when referring to the area where the school is based, we should refer to that -- I should refer to that as Cer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Cer. Cer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. There was a battalion headquarters of the HVO based at Cer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And there in the school building was a communications centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Communications centre, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: And the kitchen, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Was the battalion command based there?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Everything was there. It's a huge building built back in the former Yugoslavia. A huge building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time, and I mean in early September of 1993, there were between 100 and 150 HVO soldiers in Uzdol. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many, 150 perhaps, up to 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Now, I understand you don't have an exact figure, but is your evidence here that the range of -- that the range that you think of soldiers that were present there was between 150 and 200?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Sometimes 100, sometimes 150, depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, at that time, was there a tank based in -- an HVO owned and operated tank based in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When not actively firing at things, was that tank normally placed near to Cer and the school?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, outside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the battalion headquarters in the school at Cer, were there also various artillery positions on the hills around about, including anti-aircraft guns, Howitzers, mortars, and other equipment?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Around the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Now, in those days there were many soldiers in that battalion who were local people from the hamlets of Uzdol. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, but they weren't at the front line every day. They would have leave every two or three days before they went back to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Very well. And at that time was the leadership of the battalion -- who was the commander of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know. People said it was a man named Buza. I'm not sure what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question, and I apologise. I'll stop there. I should have made my question clearer. I meant the commander of your battalion, a battalion of HVO based in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The commander was Prskalo, Josip Prskalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He was the owner of a house that was burnt down. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. That was his father's house actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, there were -- at the school you've indicated that there was a kitchen and a communications centre as well as the command post. Is it the case that approximately ten soldiers were also billeted at that school?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were they local soldiers or were they soldiers who were the crew of the tank who would come from other places?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Some were the crew of the tank and some were from Rama, from Prozor. It was too far for them to go back home to spend the night, so they would sleep there in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Very well. So the position was this: The local soldiers would go home to their own homes to sleep, but the soldiers from Prozor or other parts --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. Scete and Rama, people from those places would usually sleep at the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. I have to ask you -- I have to go through a list of names here of various people, and I just want to ask you where you think they were accommodated, doing the best you can, I understand it's ten years ago or more, but I'd just ask you to exercise your memory as best you can. Do you recall an HVO soldier named Drago Barisic who was later killed in an action at Here?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was in Ljubunci. They were at the front line between Glibe and Jurici. He didn't come to Uzdol; it was too far for them to go. They were further down in a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Zelika Briza.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Zeljko Brizar. Brizar probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You'll have to --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Brizar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, you'll have to forgive some Australian bad pronunciation. I will promise to do my best however. But Mr. Brizar --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Where was he on the night of the 13th of September, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I have no idea. I think probably at Prozor or thereabouts, but I can't say where he was deployed along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Ilija Cvitanovic; do you recall him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Ilija from Rumboci, yes. He was in the school building at Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did he -- was he killed during the fighting on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There was a man named Cvitanovic. I'm not sure if he was him or not but it's possible. There was one man called Zelic and another called Cvitanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Those two were friends, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now pressing on and I'm taking you through -- it's a number of individuals, Fabjan Grabovac?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Fabjan Grabovac, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you say "no," is that somebody you don't recall now?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: We didn't have anyone named Grabovac. It may have one of the crew operating the tank. We don't have that kind of surname in our village. He may be part of the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I believe he was, and I'll come back to him later on.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know all the people who were there. Sometimes new people would come in. I didn't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but I have to put these names to you. If you don't recall them being there, you say so that's fine. Damir Haluzan?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Where was he that night?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Ivan Kolakusic?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Ivan Kolakusic is from Ljubunci. I'm not sure where he was that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Ivan Kovcalija and Marinko Kovcalija and Pero Kovcalija were all local people, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: From Uzdol, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was one of those persons killed on the 14th, on the morning of the 14th of September?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Pero, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Pero Kovcalija was killed. He was an active HVO soldier. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Where was he killed?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was killed outside Ante Zelic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The house has no roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. I just have some questions about him now. He was an HVO soldier. Did you see his body yourself?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Was he in uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was the first one I saw after I left Mijo Maric's house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, pardon me, I cut across you there. Was he in uniform when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he armed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. He had left the school building to check something out and he was killed right there. He was not carrying a rifle. Not far from him there was another body, a BH army soldier. I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did the BH army soldier have a weapon with him when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I can't remember whether he had a weapon or not. Maybe one of the soldiers who had withdrawn prior to that had taken his weapon. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell me, did all three Kovcalijas sleep in the same premises on that night, the 13th of September, or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. Pero was in the school building; he must have been on duty. And Ivan Kovcalija was sleeping in his house which burned down. This house belonged to the two brothers. Ivan managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What about the Marinko?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I think Marinko was at the front line near Komin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just explain whether that part of the front line is at Uzdol or is it further away?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: That is a hill above Uzdol between Lisina and Konjsko, a hill called Komin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. I want to turn to another person now, Franjo Krizanac.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Franjo Krizanac was not at Uzdol. Franjo ... He was elsewhere with the army. He did something elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Ivan Ljubic?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Ivan Ljubic lived in Uzdol. His father, Mato, had been killed as well as his wife, Kata. That morning he was at Kransko Polje as a member of the home guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As a member of the armed guard and as a local farmer, did he own a weapon?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He had some sort of rifle over at Kracko Polje. And he came with us, or rather he followed us after his wife had been killed and his house and barn had been burned down. Most of them have M-48 rifles, the old type, one each usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When you say "most of them," who do you mean by most of them? Do you mean most of the older people?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, those older people. There weren't many of them. They stood guard along the road to see that no one laid any mines for cars or vehicles using the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, pressing on with other people. Pero Lucic?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it will probably be a type writing error.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Lucic. Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think he was part of the tank crew. He must have been from Bugojno. He was killed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And did you know an Ivica Maric?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Maric, there were a lot of people called Maric. There was one who was chief of police. There was another man, a rather young man called Maric. There was several people called Ivica Maric depending on the age. I'm not sure which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were there any Ivica Marics who were living in Uzdol -- and the one I'm thinking of here is a person who was killed a couple months later early in 1994 in battle.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Josip Maric was the only Maric who was actually killed. Josip Maric, not Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Josip Maric was a soldier. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: On the 14th, yes, yes. He was killed on the 14th of September at the school, the steps outside the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: But I don't know anyone called Ivica Maric. It certainly -- not any of the people who were killed at Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just have a quick question about Slavko Mendes. How far from the school was the body of Slavko Mendes?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Mendes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. How was from the school was the body of Slavko Mendes?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Slavko was stationed in front of the school. The medical station, the post office, and the registrar's office further down from the school building, that's where they were. There's a pharmacy selling farming products nearby. The distance is perhaps 80 to 100 metres. They took him there. His hands were tied behind his back by a length of rope. He was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. You did you know Vlado Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Vlado Mijatovic, not from our village. Only he was one of the crew, but we don't have that last name in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I just want to pause there. I'll return to this list of names in a minute. I want to ask you some questions about the organisation of the defence of Uzdol by the HVO. You've indicated that there was a battalion command at the school and that battalion was the 3rd Battalion of an -- of which brigade?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The Rama Brigade. I think that's what it was called. Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. An active front line --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: But we belonged to Prozor, to Rama.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, active front line combat activities were normally carried out by regular HVO soldiers of normal fighting age. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you referred to an institution called the home guard a little earlier. Who was it who issued orders and instructions to the home guard?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know that. They had someone who was in charge. There would be two or three people standing guard at Kracko Polje at night. Every three or four days some of them would come over. And the man in charge probably reported to Prskalo, the commander. But I really can't say with any degree of certainty. I was not one of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm -- because you were there, we have to ask you these questions. At all events, although you don't know the name of the person -- you don't know the name of the -- well, I should ask you this: Do you know the name of the person who was in charge of the home guard in your area?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Our area, I think his name was Kazo Milicevic from Kranjcici. He was born in 1958. He was killed -- or rather, he had been injured seriously at a company over in Salakovac and he was handicapped, disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And so far as you understood the line of reporting and responsibility, the home guard answered to Mr. Prskalo, who was the battalion commander in Uzdol. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was the number one man. The others were probably afraid of him whenever he went to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who are you talking about there? Mr. Prskalo?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of that battalion and all the home guards had to obey him. He would give orders. Sometimes he would tour the units. Those were no real soldiers, you know, like the ones along the front line. Those were elderly people. Sometimes they would just doze off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand that. You indicated -- you gave some answers concerning weapons and those elderly people. Could I ask you this: Did the HVO army issue them with weapons or did they just use weapons that they had at the farm?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: At the beginning they used hunting rifles and then they were supplied with proper rifles. They usually had old rifles, M-48.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay, I understand that. And just to clarify that a little bit further, in peacetime Uzdol was effectively a farming area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, it was a farming area. The road is barred. It was a backward area, the middle of nowhere, like the other villages that I told you about, those local communes, Scipe and Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And it was the normal practice for local farmers to have hunting rifles simply for the purposes of protecting stock from wolves and other wild animals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. We had two hunters' associations, one at Scipe and one at Uzdol. Hunters. We would socialise before the war. Sometimes we would throw a party. We would go hunting together, that sort of thing. There were quite a number of hunters before the war. They used shotguns, sawn-off shotguns, that sort of thing. Very few people had proper carbine rifles, hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. I should ask you this question actually: Was your father one such hunter while he was alive?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. My father, myself, we had a shotgun, 16-millimetre shotgun. You have two types, a 12-millimetre shotgun and a 16-millimetre shotgun, and we had a 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you answered a little bit earlier that after the very beginning early days of the armed conflict, the army issued some older regular carbines, M-48s, to the elderly civilians that filled these roles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Some new rifles were supplied and everybody wanted to have a Kalashnikov, a modern rifle. No one wanted to have the old ones. And some were eventually given these new and better rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Okay. Now, just turning to the military situation that was in place just before the tragedies took place in Uzdol. At that time you were aware that there was the possibility -- well, I take that back. I'll put it another way. The HVO forces themselves were planning offensive operations in the area of Uzdol and perhaps a little bit further up towards Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know about that. No, not until Uzdol fell. They didn't attack and we didn't attack. They held their lines and we held ours. There was some random shooting every now and then. Sometimes one or two soldiers would be killed on their side or HVO soldiers, but there were no fierce attacks, no fierce fighting until the 14th. There were random incursions, attacks, against the Vakuf and the front lines further down. As for Komin and Here and the lines that we held, there was nothing much happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to be very clear about the specific. Is it your evidence that you had no knowledge of a forthcoming attack by the HVO against Bosnian army positions, such attack due to be carried out on the 14th of September or very soon afterwards?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell us anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, were you also aware that there was the possibility of an attack by the Bosnian army in the neighbourhood of Uzdol on the 13th or 14th of September or very shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Nothing happened before the 13th, and then on the 13th and 14th I was in Prozor. There was an announcement that they would attack Crni Vrh in the area of Makljen, those lines over there. That morning Uzdol was attacked and then the army went to Crni Vrh because Uzdol received reinforcements from Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But my questions really relate to what you were told before these attacks took place. Were you told by your superiors that there was the possibility of an attack by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in your sector?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Had I known about it, obviously I would have taken my family away, my father, my mother, and my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, my next question -- you've already answered my next question by that answer. My next question is this: That the command post of the 3rd Battalion was screened from actual the front line by the villages Kriz, Rajici, and the other hamlets where these killings took place. Is that correct? In other words, those villages where the tragedies happened were between the command post of the 3rd Battalion and the front line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: These villages were effectively in the front line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, no, they were between the lines because the line was up there. From Zelenike you have Komin about two or three kilometres away. That's the line near the village, but they didn't attack the line. They entered the space in between. And as Borak near Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But what I --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Borak is closer to Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think it might be appropriate that I show you a document here. I'm sorry, no, I might delay that. I'll have to get a particular photocopy made before I show you that document. So just excuse me for a moment. All right. Just in terms of the situation on the front line, though, that was the position: There were villages that were exclusively Muslim which included the villages of Here, Scipe, and Kute. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. There were Croats in Scipe, it's a mixed village. And there was Grubesas also up there, and Here -- well, the population wasn't mixed there. And the village of Skarice belonged to Kute. There were two or three houses there in Skara that belonged to village Kute, but Here wasn't mixed. In Scipe there was Grubesas, Markici. Those are the Croatian parts. And towards Salakovac there was Ivanci and Pajici. And there's Banja Lucica further down which is also part -- which also comes under my office, but Ivanci, Pajici, and Banjici are purely Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you were not present in Uzdol when the actual fighting and killing took place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. My wife had a child that morning; I remained there that evening and that's when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. By the time you came to the village it was already daylight -- I'm sorry, by the time you came to Uzdol it was already daylight. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, it was daylight. The ABiH had already left Uzdol and left in the direction of Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And by the time you got there do you recall whether there was still heavy firing of artillery or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There was firing, mortar fire. I don't know who was firing. You couldn't see much because of the smoke, but there was sporadic firing from the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And even at the time when you were there, visibility over long distances was somewhat obscured by smoke from the burning buildings which you've described. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The livestock was on fire, too, so there was a stench the air in the stables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, what I'm going to do is take you through the -- through your actions when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could first of all be shown a photograph. I think it's MFI 298.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What you're going to be shown here, Mr. Zelenika, is a panoramic view I think of the Uzdol neighbourhood taken from the neighbourhood of the school. Now -- very well. I just like --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be assisted with the marker pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zelenika, some of the things I ask you about might not be perfectly visible on the photograph, but I really want a general picture of your movements. So could you just indicate, please, where -- after you arrived at the school and when you set off to go around the villages, could you just use a dotted line and indicate the direction that you went from the school to go around the villages and look?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I came out here. There's a house down here below, and then I came out here. We didn't take this road towards Rajici, but we crossed over near the school. This is where I saw Pero Kovcalija by the house that doesn't have a roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just put a 1.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And continue on with the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Then I continued on in this direction and there was a Bosniak soldier here, an ABiH soldier. I then continued in this direction. And here you can see the monument erected to Slavko Mendes. And then I continued to this house here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop for one second. Would you put a 2 where Slavko Mendes was.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Number 2, that's near.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Just keep going as you did.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Number 3 is where Ivo was and what was her name? Ivka and Zora was here in the woods in the vicinity of the house. And I continued in this direction. And here I found Mate Ljubic and Kata Ljubic. The road then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Stop for one moment please --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: -- continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The two houses you've just indicated where you saw Ivo and so on, what's that called? Is that the start of Zelenike or what's the name of that area?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It's all called Cer, the school, the two houses here, and this house that was a chemists before the war. It isn't open now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So really the -- where Ivo, Domin, Ivka, and Zorka were --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: That's all -- the entire area is called Cer. Right up to the church it's Cer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's just going to -- it will assist the Tribunal now and later on if we can say where the killed people were killed, and I'm sorry to take you through it in detail again, but it's important. So anyway, Ivo, Domin, Ivka are at Cer and so also is Mato and Kata Ljubic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, they're also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, you proceed.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The road continues here up to Perkovici. This is their old house, and Stipo and Kata lived there. Kata was killed and Stipo survived. He died later on at his son's in Dubrovnik. He had two sons in Dubrovnik. This is the new son, Perkovici, and the son Slavko lives there. No one lives in the old house in which Kata was killed now. It's number 5, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's correct. Keep going, yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: 5. And this house is Kovcalija, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before we get to that, could you just keep the dotted line going, showing the path that you took in general terms.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The road goes in this direction and this is Mara's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I ask you to stop for one second, please. Where you've drawn that zigzagging line, what's the name of that village there? Is that Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: That's Zelenike, and at the top we have Zelici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Have I stopped you at the point where you went past Zelici?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: When I returned from Zelici down below where I found Stipo Marici and the wife, we didn't use the same path to return; we used a different route.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, I understand that. Could I stop you there. Would you just mark please with an X that is visible there where you saw the two young children on the road, young Stjepan in particular.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Now, I'll ask you to continue in a moment, but just for future reference to make it easy, do you see the red numbers in the top corner of the screen on the right-hand side? It's says 0402 --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I see the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just between --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Between those numbers and the red line you've drawn, would you mind writing the word "Zelenike" quite small there.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excellent. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This is Cer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Please do write Cer.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you continue with the road that you took?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: And there is a road that goes this way. We have Budim here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Stop for one moment at Budimi. Is Budimi a very small hamlet?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It's a hamlet with three or four houses up to the cemetery. Our cemetery is up here. We then followed the road in this way, passed through these meadows and reached Ante Stojanovic's house in Kriz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you just write -- well -- keep drawing the path that you took and then I'll get you to write "Kriz" over there.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There's a hill here so you go around the hill. This is where Stojanovic's house is; you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In corner above there's the village of Bobari, a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for one moment. I just want to clarify something here. In this photograph is it possible to see the whole of the village of Kriz or is it concealed?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, you can't. There's a hill so you can only see Brko's or Ante Stojanovic's house, and an old house at the top. But the other village, the village faces Krstiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is write the word "Kriz" there where the village is, even though we know it's on the other side of that hill.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There's a road now that goes to Franjo's house. It goes around the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Now, before we go any further, could you explain to the Court what is the name of the big hill that you can see in the distance there and to the right?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: To the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: In the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean on the horizon. There's quite a high hill there.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: At the top there's a kill we call Konsko, that's the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you indicate -- don't write anything yet, but I'll get you to do a mark in a minute. But on that photograph the hill of Krstiste is on the right -- is out of the photograph on the right-hand side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: To the right you can see Here and this hill continues in this direction, and below there was Borak. Our line was there. There was a house up there above the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just to assist when people come to look at this drawing later on - it's going to be a very helpful drawing - and I wonder if you would write "Krstiste," naming the hill and point an arrow in the direction where Krstiste is to be found. Maybe write it up near those numbers 04020894 and then draw an arrow pointing to where Krstiste is. Now I'm sorry about --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Krstiste. That's on the hill here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now, that's enough of Krstiste. Could you just continue with the line that you took. Just continue drawing the dotted line where you went. I understand you were out of sight --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: We were here by this village and then we returned. We took this route. We continued in this direction, and the road passes behind the church.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Would you mark in now on that map where Rajici is, please?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And is the area where the two churches are considered to be part of Rajici or part of Cer?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The churches?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Up in between. You have the houses in Cer and the old school down below, the school that you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Now, would you please mark the village of Here.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The village of Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: There's the Croatian village of Pale here. This is the village of Pale. It was a Croatian village, and it's been burnt down. There's nothing there now. Bobari is here. Bobari, Pribucak there's quite a number of hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We won't be concerned with Bobari at the moment. But would you just mark in --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: This is Kucari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you mind just marking in -- writing in the name Budimi where that is?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Budimi, here it is, between Kriz and Zelenike, there's a stream there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So Budimi is quite a low-lying village in that terrain. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It's quite high up. Mendes is down below. We passed through Budimi, so we didn't mention Mendes. There's a little hamlet, two houses, and it's called Mendes. There's Mendes, Josip; Mendes, Zora. There are three or four of them. But nothing was burned down there. Only the first stable that belonged to Zora right near the road to Rajici was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Do you recall -- when you were walking -- sorry, I'll stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit D314.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zelenika, I've just lost my place. Here we are. All right. I want to take you to some of the incidents upon which you -- some of the things that you noticed when you walked around that path you've indicated to us. And the first thing I want to do is take you to the village of Kriz, when you got to Kriz. Do you recall as you got to the foot of the hill at Kriz that you came to the house of Ante Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And Ante is the person who had the nickname of Brko because of his moustache. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was called Brko because he would have a small moustache. He used to wear a short moustache, but that was his nickname, Brko, moustache, probably because of his moustache. He worked in Austria, Germany, and he was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at that point did you notice a surviving person called Ivka Stojanovic emerge?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: About 30 to 50 metres away from where Brko was there was a sort of borderline area where two meadows join each other and there was some plum trees there, some thorny bushes, et cetera, and that's where we found Ivka Zelenika, or rather Stojanovic, but Zelenika was her maiden name. We found her in the underbrush there because she was Luca's daughter and she got married to Nevenko Stojanovic in Kriz. He is in Austria and is now retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was she -- I've got some questions about Ivka and what happened with Ivka there. When Ivka came out -- can I ask you, are you personally related to Ivka in any way?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Because my father and Ivka were the children of two brothers. Ivka's mother was my parent's aunt and Ivka's father was my father's uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And did Ivka have at that time or does she have a son?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: She has a son Janko he was wounded then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Ivka thought that he had been killed, but he hadn't been killed. I told her that the mother had been killed. She was worried about Janko more than about her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'll come to that conversation in just a moment. I just wanted to establish some relationships first before I ask you about it. And at that time how old was her son, Janko, who she was worried about?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Well, he was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: But that morning -- well, he was over 20 years old. He's now married, lives in Zagreb, but I don't know when he was born exactly. He has a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. I won't -- you've answered the question satisfactorily, thank you. Anyway, when Ivka came out she told you that her son had saved her by shooting at the enemy while she got away. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, she doesn't remember that. All she says is she doesn't know anything. Someone came across her when she fell down on the path and someone trampled on her apparently, but she thought that he had remained in the village of Mrdana [phoen]. He hadn't remained there, he fled, down below. You can see this in the photograph. He descended from Kriz down to Polje and then fled in the direction of Prozor. And Ivka couldn't remember anything. She was scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Look, I understand that. Could I just ask you, the video that you've just looked at that the Prosecutor showed you. You were shown that video of course before giving evidence here in the Tribunal. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Were you shown the whole thing or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, not the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Apart from --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's a part which -- were you shown the excerpts which were shown in court today and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I saw them, yes. Others I wasn't shown but only briefly. I have been shown far more today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Sorry, just to clarify that, you were shown more today than what you've seen in proofing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: The images of Stipe really affected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to show you the images of Stipe and I'm not going to show you any images from your own home, so you can be rest assured of that. But I have some images now that I'm going to have to show you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would just ask that the witness be shown the section of the audio/visual tape commencing at 40.34, and it will take about three minutes of time. Sorry, just excuse me, that will have to be cued up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What we're going to show you now so you know what's coming is a part of the video where Ivka Stojanovic appears and speaks. And I'll get you to look at that and then I'll ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I indicate that the part that I want played is we think at 40.34. The screen is indicating a later stage at this point. So unfortunately I think the cue might have been jumped. So it's 40.34 that we want if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honours, this is not the passage that we want to have played to the witness. Might Your Honour excuse me, I'm going to make an inquiry as to where the difficulty might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's listed in paragraph 48, 43.14. Instead of 40.34 it should be 43.14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that assistance from the Prosecution. Perhaps that could be tried. Your Honours, it's at page 16, 17, and 18 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Ivka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's far enough. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Before I ask you some questions about that, I just want to raise a matter with the Tribunal now, Mr. Zelenika. Just excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution have provided us with a transcript of this tape in full long ago. The complete transcript has of course been provided. I take it that that would be part of the exhibit with the tape, but I didn't clarify that at the time. Perhaps I could just clarify that with my learned friend now, whether that's a part of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection. For completeness it should go in with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. Generally speaking, the transcript will go with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Rather than having a separate exhibit, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But could we be furnished with that part of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Otherwise it will lead us to nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was under the mistake that there would be a simultaneous translation of that. I'm sorry. It's certainly not the interpreters' fault in the booth. I just had achieved a state of mind that it was going to happen. It's my fault. In fact, I should have ensured it. But what I'll do is ask the witness some questions. I'll indicate too that I'll provide, we'll provide copies of the entire transcript and, in particular, of the pages which we've referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, my sorry, my hand-fistedness has caused a delay there, but now I can ask you some questions. You haven't seen that part of the tape for many years, if ever. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, I simply didn't want to. I knew the tape existed, but I refused to see it. This was tough enough for me now. There were tapes about Prozor, too, some people watched those tapes but I refused to. My wife refused to. And I didn't want my children to see these tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We can understand that and that's okay. But now that you've seen that tape you agree that Ivka Stojanovic made it perfectly plain that she got away because her son fired shots to save her. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in Prozor at the time when her son escaped. I met him down by the Stojanovic's house; he had already escaped. We only found her later in the afternoon in that thicket up on the hill. I wasn't in Kriz. He must have been in the house. He probably hadn't been on duty that morning, but I can't tell you how he managed to escape. We found him near this border between the two meadows, and we found the son on our way from Prozor back to Uzdol, and another person, too, named Fabjan Ratkic. He is Martin and Kata's son. He ran across the field. They were just running, Fabjan and Janko as well, running towards Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand what you say about that. But you watched Ivka on the screen then and first of all you can tell the Tribunal here that that was Ivka, wasn't it, that you just saw?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And when you listened on the screen then you heard Ivka saying: "My name is Ivka Stojanovic." And then you heard her saying: "In the house" -- you heard her being asked, Ivka Stojanovic, "where were you when these" -- and she said: "In the house. One called me to go up there. Come, Grandma, come up here. I will not harm you. Then I just -- then I fell. I don't know what else to do. Someone stepped on me, who it was, I don't know. I rolled down while crawling into those thorny shrubs." Do you remember her saying that on the tape?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. But she didn't fall down outside her house. She fell down where we found her, near the other house near the thicket. She was running away, and she probably fell down at some point and someone knocked her down, but it was closer to the Rajic's house. There's a slope there, and I believe that's where she fell down. We found her nearer Brko's house than her own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. I understand what you say. But what I'm asking about now is what you've seen on that tape and what you heard her saying. And you recall that she was then asked on the tape: "And did you have anyone else in the house?" And she said: "Yes, I did." And then a male voice said: "Son Janko?" And she said: "My son Janko was there." And my question to you is: You heard her saying that on the tape a minute ago just a minute ago, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. Janko was a soldier. He had not been an duty that morning. He'd been on leave but he had to flee his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, but I just want to go on with what you heard said on the tape. You remember she was asked the question: "Was he also in the house?" And Ivka said: "Poor thing, down there he fired behind the corner. I yelled, Mato yelled. He said, Here they come into the village from Rajici" -- it's written Ratkici here but anyway. "Here they come into the village from Rajici" --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Ratkici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. Then she yelled: "Run mom, I will shoot so that you can go. I don't know about anyone else anymore." Now, you heard her say that on the tape, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know. I wasn't there when her son was there, when she was running. She must have stayed in the thicket for about four or five hours until we found her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But even on the day when you spoke to her you had the information that her son had been shooting in the neighbourhood of her house at the invading forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I don't remember who said what once we got there. She's a relative of mine. I saw that she was scared. She didn't say anything to me. I have no idea what happened in their house because where we found her was quite a distance from their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, her son, you've indicated, was not on duty that day. Was it your understanding that he had spent the night in her house?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had spent the night in the house. Maybe he'd been at the front line and he only arrived early in the morning, but I really can't say because I was in Prozor myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he in uniform when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: He was in uniform. He was running maybe 30 or 40 metres ahead of me. His name was Ivan Mehuric. I knew him and I knew Fabjan but I was nowhere near hem. We were on our way to Mijo Maric's house, and they ran from Kriz straight down the slope. But I knew them and their names were Janko and Fabjan Ratkic. I believe they're still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was Fabjan in uniform when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how long -- and when was it that you saw these two boys or these two men Fabjan and Janko? Was that before you met with Ivka or later on?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Before we found her. The soldiers were all sleeping there in uniform. Whenever they were off duty they still had to be in uniform, where we were wearing civilian clothes ourselves. So it was very obvious. A soldier always had to be a soldier, had to remain a soldier, and they were not allowed to wear civilian clothes at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Were you wearing civilian clothes when you came to the village?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, I was wearing a uniform. I was not allowed to wear civilian clothes. You were forbidden as a soldier to wear civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But when you were off duty you were required to keep your personal weapon and some ammunition with you, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. You had to keep your personal ammunition. You would go to the cowshed to look after your livestock. You would take them over to the creek to give them water and then you would tie them up right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So when you took -- when you were off duty and you were dealing with the livestock, was it your -- I'm asking you about your personal custom now. When you were off duty and you were dealing with your own livestock, was it your practice to carry the weapon with you for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes. You can't go down the road without a rifle. What sort of a soldier would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no. But even when you were off duty, that was your practice, wasn't it, to take the weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Yes, I would take it home, I would leave it there, and you would go and do something else. You would help out your father, your mother. You didn't have the rifle on you all the time, but if you were leaving the front line you had to bring your rifle with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it did happen from time to time that you would have other pieces of military equipment with you such as hand grenades. Is that correct? And I mean even when you were off duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I didn't have hand grenades, not ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But it was well and truly within your knowledge that other people in the village did have hand grenades in their house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: Every soldier would sign for a number of hand grenades. Sometimes there was a shortage of these, so people didn't have them. And sometimes people used them. This was not a proper army, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, I -- I understand that, but I just have to do -- I have to ask you to deal with my specific question here. It was well and truly within your knowledge, wasn't it, that some people in the village had hand grenades in their house? Now, is the answer to that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He said "some people." Is he referring to soldiers? Is he referring to civilians? Is he referring to the people at the school? This is a matter he should be more specific with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, could we have clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I certainly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Then we'll break for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's in your knowledge, isn't it, that some civilians in the village had hand grenades in their house? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know about that. If a soldier comes to his father's house with a hand grenade, they may give the hand grenade to their father, or they may not. This is not something I can speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I want you to be very careful about this. You know of at least one case, don't you, where a civilian person in your village had hand grenades and used hand grenades on the morning when these killings took place. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I know that a hand grenade was thrown near old Ruza Zelic's house. I have no idea who threw the grenade, whether it was the soldiers or someone else. I have no idea who -- I saw a whole there and later we found two casings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you find any hand grenades in the trousers of young Stipo when those trousers were found?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No. It was a tracksuit that he wore, but he was naked when we found him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But in those trousers, though, when they were found, were there hand grenades there, those tracksuit pants?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I don't know. It was just a regular tracksuit. I didn't exactly search it. When I came down, I realised that the tracksuit had been left hanging on a shrub beside the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But it was told to you quite plainly that there were hand grenades in that tracksuit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: It's a very small tracksuit worn by a child. The pocket isn't big enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were you told that information or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't nor did I see that. The soldiers chasing Stipo and his mother Marija dropped a magazine used for an automatic rifle and a hand grenade near the thicket. It was a black hand grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, let's be very clear about something here: Your honest evidence before this Tribunal is that you know nothing about Ruza Zelic throwing hand grenades. Is that the fact?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA
utterances.text: I'm not sure now whether it was Ruza or the soldiers, and when she ran I'm not sure whether she actually had a hand grenade on her or not or, if so, whether she actually knew how to use it. There are soldiers around who don't know how to use a hand grenade and she was a lady after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That might be an appropriate moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, I'm afraid that you have to stay in The Hague for another day. And as I did to other witnesses, you are now under the oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
